ideas.title: What learners expect now: the consumer trends reshaping training
ideas.standfirst: People learn from YouTube before breakfast, use AI tools their employer never gave them, and choose jobs partly on how much they will grow. This digest gathers the research on what learners now expect from training, and what that means for the courses and retreats you design.

short.heading: The short version
items: **Learning has gone consumer.** People already teach themselves from video and search, on their own time. Training now competes with free, instant, good-enough help.
**AI arrived before the training did.** Three in four knowledge workers said they used AI at work in 2024, and most brought their own tools. People expect help that is personal and immediate.

**Growth matters more than ladders.** Younger workers rank learning among the top reasons they choose an employer, but few aim for senior leadership. They want skills, progress and practice on real work.
**People still want people.** The same surveys rate mentoring, peer learning and learning on the job above formal courses. That is the opening for live, human, well-designed experiences.

p: **People teach themselves, constantly.** In a 2018 Pew Research Center survey, about half of US adults who use YouTube said it was very important for figuring out how to do things they had not done before. A survey commissioned by Google across ten European countries found 64% felt YouTube helped them learn skills for personal or professional advancement. That second figure comes from YouTube's owner, so treat it as a signal rather than a measurement.

**The bar is set outside work.** Consumer research by McKinsey in 2021 found that 71% of consumers expected companies to personalise their interactions, and 76% were frustrated when that did not happen. That was about shopping, not learning. But the people on your course are the same people, and a generic, one-size course feels dated to them in the way a generic advert does.

**Personal does not mean learning styles.** The useful kind of personalisation is by role, prior knowledge and goal. Sorting people by preferred style does not hold up. There is more on [the big myths](t:1.10) and on [finding out who is in the room](t:1.29).

sections.h: AI arrived before the training did
p: **Most knowledge workers already use it.** Microsoft and LinkedIn's 2024 survey of 31,000 people in 31 countries found 75% of knowledge workers said they used generative AI at work, and 78% of those users brought their own tools rather than waiting for their employer. In Deloitte's 2025 survey of younger workers, about three-quarters expected generative AI to change how they work within a year.

**Expectations shift with it.** People who can ask an AI tool to explain something at eleven at night will expect training to give quick answers and save live time for what a tool cannot do: practice, judgement and feedback from people. There is more on [designing an AI literacy and adoption programme](t:7.14).

**Learning helps people choose an employer.** Deloitte's 2025 survey of 23,482 Gen Z and millennial workers in 44 countries found learning and development among the top three reasons they chose their current employer. Only 6% said their main career goal was a leadership position.

**Career progress drives learning.** LinkedIn's 2025 Workplace Learning Report names progress towards career goals as people's top motivation to learn. Learning that shows where it leads competes better for attention than learning that does not.

**Practice and mentors rank highest.** In Deloitte's survey, 88% of Gen Zs and 89% of millennials said on-the-job learning and practical experience mattered for their development, and more than 80% rated mentoring, peer learning and feedback as helpful. Formal training programmes were on the list too, but not at the top.

**Experiences are a growing market.** Pine and Gilmore argued in 1998 that experiences are a distinct economic offering, beyond goods and services. The Global Wellness Institute put wellness tourism at about US$982 billion in 2025, up 11.4% in a year. One detail matters for a training business: in its 2025 report, workplace wellness was the only wellness market that shrank, by 1.5% from 2023 to 2024. Buyers are paying for experiences that do something, not for wellbeing perks.

**This is the opening for well-designed live learning.** Free content covers information. What people value and cannot get from a video is practice with feedback, people to learn with, and time that is protected for it. There is more on [the case for taking people away](insight:why-take-people-away).

mind.heading: Things to bear in mind
items: **Most of these figures are surveys.** They show what people say and expect, not what changes their learning.
**Several come from vendors.** Microsoft, LinkedIn, Google and McKinsey all have products or services to sell. Use their figures, and say whose they are.
**Generations overlap.** Differences between age groups in work attitudes are small, so design for the job and the person, not the birth year. There is more on [the big myths](t:1.10).
**Personalisation can go wrong.** Tailoring by role and prior knowledge helps. Tailoring by learning style does not.
**Expectations are not evidence.** People expecting short, instant learning does not mean short, instant learning works for complex skills. Give people what works, in a form that respects their time.

business.heading: What this means for your offer
p: **Do not compete with free content.** Curate it, and spend live time on practice, feedback and people.
**Personalise by role and goal.** Ask about people's work and level before you design, and show each person where the learning leads.
**Assume people already use AI.** Teach good use, and design the parts of the course AI cannot do.
**Sell experiences with results.** Buyers are cutting wellbeing perks and still paying for experiences that change how people work. Lead with the result.

ideas.title: Attention is the scarce resource: what learners expect now, and how to hold it
ideas.standfirst: Is there e-learning fatigue? Are attention spans really shrinking? What do people want from training when their working day is broken into two-minute pieces? This digest gathers the research, separates what is measured from what is repeated, and ends with what holds attention in a session today.

short.heading: The short version
items: **Attention spans have not been shown to collapse.** The eight-second goldfish figure has no source. What has been measured is that people switch between screens far more often than they used to: on average every 47 seconds in recent studies, against about two and a half minutes in 2004.

**The working day is the problem.** Heavy users of Microsoft 365 are interrupted about every two minutes in core hours, and fewer than four in ten learning professionals say employees get time away from their job to learn. Learners arrive fragmented and short of time.

**"E-learning fatigue" is real in parts.** Video-call fatigue is measured and well described. Low completion of long, open online courses is measured. Fatigue with digital learning as such is mostly anecdote, and well-designed online learning teaches as well as a classroom.

**Attention is held by design, not by length.** Active tasks, short recall checks between segments, short videos, protected time and a clear link to the learner's own progress all have research behind them. A stopwatch rule does not.

p: **The goldfish figure has no source.** The claim that people now have an eight-second attention span, shorter than a goldfish, spread from a 2015 marketing report by Microsoft Canada. The report took the figure from a website called Statistic Brain, and journalists who traced it found no research behind it. In a 2022 King's College London survey, half of UK adults still believed it. There is more on [testing a claim before you repeat it](t:1.11).

**What has been measured is switching.** Gloria Mark and colleagues have logged how long office workers stay on one screen before moving to another. In 2004 it was about two and a half minutes. By about 2012 it was 75 seconds, and in studies from 2016 onwards it averaged 47 seconds. That measures how often people switch at work, with email and messages always open. It does not measure whether people can concentrate when the setting allows it.

**People feel more distracted.** In the King's College survey, 49% said their attention span felt shorter than it used to be and 23% disagreed. The researchers point out that without long-term studies nobody can say whether attention spans have actually declined. Feeling distracted is still real, and it is what learners bring into the room.

**There is no fixed span to design to.** A review of lecture studies found no good evidence for a limit of ten to fifteen minutes, and attention varied more with the teacher than with the format. There is more on [attention and mind wandering](t:1.33).

sections.h: The working day learners come from
p: **Interruptions are constant for many office workers.** Microsoft's 2025 analysis of anonymised Microsoft 365 data found the most heavily contacted fifth of users were interrupted by a meeting, email or message about every two minutes during core hours, around 275 times across a full day. Reports often quote it as the average worker. Microsoft's own note says it describes that heavily contacted group.

**Time to learn is scarce.** In the CIPD's 2023 survey of 1,108 learning professionals, 51% said people managers encourage participation in learning, but only 39% said employees are given time away from their day-to-day role to take part. LinkedIn's 2025 Workplace Learning Report found managers and employees too stretched to focus on development, and only 15% of employees said their manager had helped them build a career plan in the previous six months.

**Career progress is why people choose to learn.** The same LinkedIn report names progress towards career goals as people's number one motivation to learn. Learning that shows how it moves someone forward competes better for scarce attention than learning that does not. There is more on [why people value a task](t:1.34).

**Video-call fatigue is measured.** Researchers at Stanford built a scale for it and surveyed 10,591 people. More daily video calling went with more fatigue. Women reported more than men, with about one in seven women feeling very or extremely fatigued after calls against about one in twenty men, partly because they had longer meetings with shorter breaks and partly because of seeing themselves on screen all day. There is more on [designing against video-call fatigue](t:4.8).

**Long, open online courses lose most people.** Data from Harvard and MIT's open online courses showed completion rates stayed low and did not improve over six years, and most learners did not come back after their first year. These were free, optional courses, so low completion partly reflects people sampling and leaving. Workplace e-learning that is required gets completed, which says nothing about whether it was learned.

**Video holds attention for a few minutes.** A study of 6.9 million video sessions on edX found engagement dropped sharply after about six minutes, and that videos with a personal feel held people better than polished studio lectures.

**Digital learning as such is not the problem.** When online and classroom courses use the same methods, they teach facts equally well. What tires people is long, passive, screen-based time added to an already crowded day. The answer is better design and protected time, not a retreat from digital. There is more on [comparing online and classroom](t:3.25) and on [completion figures](t:6.7).

**Make people do something.** A pooling of 225 studies in university science courses found that students in traditional lectures were 1.5 times more likely to fail than students in courses with active learning, and exam scores were about 6% higher with active learning.

**Put a short recall check between segments.** In an online lecture experiment, people who answered a short quiz after each segment reported mind wandering at 19% of checks, against 41% for people who were not tested, and they learned more.

**Keep videos short and personal.** Cut recorded input into pieces of a few minutes, and use the live time for interaction. There is more on [blending on purpose](t:3.6) and on [keeping live time for interaction](t:4.10).

**Protect the time, not just the content.** Learning booked into the gaps of a fragmented day loses to the next message. Ask the manager to protect it, close email for the session, and say plainly why.
**Show the link to the learner's own progress.** In the first five minutes, say what people will be able to do and why it matters for their work and career.
**Plan the energy of the day.** Put demanding work where energy is highest and change the activity when it drops. There is more on [putting the hard content where the energy is](t:2.14).

items.name: The ten-minute rule
items.offers: "Change activity every ten minutes."
items.note: A review of lecture studies found no good primary evidence for a limit of ten to fifteen minutes (Bradbury, 2016).
items.mind: Change the activity when the content or the room needs it, not when the clock says.
links: Put the hard content where the energy is

mind.heading: Things to bear in mind
items: **Check what a figure measures.** Screen switching is not concentration, a survey of learning professionals is not a survey of learners, and the heaviest fifth of email users is not the average worker.

**Vendor reports have something to sell.** LinkedIn, Microsoft and platform providers publish useful data, and every report also makes a case for their product. Use the figures, and say who produced them.
**Completion is not learning.** High completion of required e-learning and low completion of free courses both say more about the setting than about what people learned.
**Most of the attention research uses students.** Workplace evidence is thinner. Treat the methods as good bets and check them with your own groups.
**Fatigue is a design signal, not a learner failing.** When people drift, change the format, the length or the time of day before you blame the audience.

business.heading: What this means for the training you design
p: **Design for people who arrive fragmented.** Open by settling the room: phones away for a reason, one clear goal, and a first task within ten minutes. There is more on [designing for people who arrive distracted](t:4.22).
**Spend live time on doing.** Put information into short recordings and reading, and use the time together for practice, discussion and feedback.

**Sell protected time as part of the offer.** Ask clients to block the time, brief managers and keep the session free of email. A training retreat takes this to its limit, which is part of [the case for taking people away](insight:why-take-people-away).
**Keep a running file of the research.** The figures here will date. Recheck the annual reports each year and add new studies as they appear.

ideas.title: The neuroscience of the retreat: what the brain science supports, and what it does not
ideas.standfirst: Retreat brochures are full of brains: cortisol falling, dopamine rising, the default mode network switching on, oxytocin bonding the team. This piece checks each claim against the research, so you can talk about the brain honestly, and know when to stop.

short.heading: The short version
items: **The behaviour is better evidenced than the brain.** Sleep, stress, reflection, novelty and moving together have useful research behind them. The brain pictures in brochures usually go well beyond it.
**Some brain stories are real but small.** Time in nature, exercise and stress all affect thinking, with modest, short-lived effects in laboratory studies of students.
**Some are hype.** "Oxytocin builds trust" did not survive scrutiny. "Dopamine hits" and "amygdala hijack" are metaphors, not findings.
**Say what happens, not what the brain does.** "Time to sleep between sessions" is honest and true. "Rewires your brain" is neither.

p: **A brain picture makes any claim look scientific.** Brain language sounds precise and is hard for a buyer to check, which is why it spreads through training and wellness marketing. There is more on [why smart people believe brain myths](t:1.9). The test is simple: does the claim tell you to do something different from what the behavioural research already says? If not, the brain story adds risk and nothing else.

**Stress affects memory, in both directions.** A pooling of 113 studies with 6,216 people found that stress shortly before or during learning usually impaired memory, unless it came very close to the learning and was related to it. Stress just after learning often improved memory. Stress just before recall impaired it. Long-running stress is a different matter and harms learning. There is more on [taking needless stress out of the room](t:1.13).

**Brochure cortisol figures are usually wrong.** This site traced one infographic claiming nature cuts cortisol "by up to 38%". The values on its chart were about a hundred times too high to be saliva measurements. Small studies do find lower stress hormone levels after time in nature, but no study supports a headline percentage for a retreat.

sections.h: Rest and the default mode network
p: **There is a brain network for turning inward.** A review by Immordino-Yang and colleagues describes the default mode network, which is active when people rest and let their minds wander. It links that network to recalling memories, imagining the future and reflecting on meaning. The review draws mostly on correlational research and argues for more study, not for a particular method.

**The useful lesson is behavioural.** Time to reflect helps learning, and experiments on reflection support it without any brain imaging. A retreat that builds in quiet time and prompts for reflection is doing the right thing. Saying it "activates the default mode network" adds nothing a buyer can use. There is more on [giving people time alone to reflect](t:8.30).

**New places may help memory.** An influential model by Lisman and Grace describes a loop in which novelty detected by the hippocampus triggers dopamine that helps new information get stored. Animal studies show that exploring a new environment strengthens memory processes. A small number of human studies, some in virtual reality, find that exploring something new improves recall.

**The leap to retreats is a long one.** The human studies are small laboratory experiments. They support the idea that a new setting is no barrier to learning and may help a little. They do not support "dopamine hits" as a selling point. There is more on [making people curious before you tell them](t:1.26).

**Oxytocin is not a trust switch.** A critical review by Nave, Camerer and McCullough found that the best-known finding, that sniffing oxytocin increases trust, has not replicated well. They concluded the evidence does not reliably link oxytocin to human trust. Drop it from any pitch.

**Moving together has better support.** Pooled experiments on moving in time with others, such as walking, rowing or dancing together, found medium effects on helpful behaviour and small to medium effects on feeling bonded. Some researchers warn that expectations may explain part of it. It is a behavioural finding and needs no brain story.

**Awe may turn attention outward.** Piff and colleagues ran five studies in which feeling awe, including in front of tall trees, went with more generous and helpful behaviour. The authors link it to a feeling of a smaller self. It is a reasonable reason to take people somewhere beautiful, stated modestly.

**Sleep is the strongest brain story.** Memories are strengthened and reorganised during sleep, and a lost night before or after learning weakens memory. A retreat that protects sleep has the brain on its side. There is more on [protecting sleep](t:1.12).

**Exercise and nature help a little.** One bout of exercise has a small, real effect on thinking. Time in nature brings small, short-lived gains in some measures of attention. Both are worth building in. Neither is a reason to promise better learning. There is more on [using nature and daylight](t:1.16).

dashboard.heading: The claims at a glance
dashboard.intro: The brain claims most often attached to retreats, how strong the research is, and what to say instead.

items.name: Stress and memory
items.offers: "Stress kills learning."
items.note: Stress before or during learning usually impaired memory; stress just after learning often helped; stress before recall impaired it (Shields and colleagues, 2017).
items.mind: Remove needless stress, especially before practice and recall. Short challenge is not the enemy.
links: Take needless stress out of the room

items.name: Cortisol percentages
items.offers: "Nature cuts stress hormones by 38%."
items.note: The figure traced on this site had chart values about a hundred times too high for saliva. Small studies do find lower stress hormone levels after time in nature.
items.mind: Drop the number. Say that time outdoors helps people recover.
links: Take people out of their routine, and plan the return

items.name: Sleep and memory
items.offers: "Sleep consolidates learning."
items.note: A lost night before learning weakens taking it in, and a lost night after weakens keeping it (Newbury and colleagues, 2021; Diekelmann and Born, 2010).
items.mind: The strongest brain claim you can make. Back it by protecting sleep in the timetable.
links: Protect sleep on multi-day programmes

items.name: Default mode network
items.offers: "Retreats switch on the brain's reflective network."
items.note: The network active at rest is linked to memory, imagining the future and reflection, in mostly correlational research (Immordino-Yang and colleagues, 2012).
items.mind: Build in reflection. Leave the network out of the brochure.
links: Give people time alone to reflect

items.name: Novelty and dopamine
items.offers: "New places release dopamine that boosts learning."
items.note: A strong model (Lisman and Grace, 2005) and animal studies, with a few small human experiments finding better recall after exploring something new.
items.mind: A new setting may help a little. "Dopamine hits" is marketing.
links: Make people curious before you tell them

items.name: Oxytocin and trust
items.offers: "Bonding releases oxytocin, the trust hormone."
items.note: The evidence does not reliably link oxytocin to human trust (Nave, Camerer and McCullough, 2015).
items.mind: Remove it. Build trust with the methods that work: safety, time and shared work.
links: Build trust before you ask for openness

items.name: Moving together
items.offers: "Moving in time together bonds a group."
items.note: Pooled experiments found a medium effect of moving in time together on helpful attitudes and behaviour (Rennung and Göritz, 2016). Expectations may explain part of it.
items.mind: Group walks and movement may help people bond. Keep them optional.
links: Offer movement sessions people can choose

items.name: Awe
items.offers: "Awe makes people more generous."
items.note: Feeling awe, including in front of tall trees, went with more generous and helpful behaviour (Piff and colleagues, 2015).
items.mind: A modest reason to choose a beautiful setting. Not a promise of a changed team.
links: Use the outdoors on a retreat, on purpose

items.name: Nature and attention
items.offers: "Nature restores the brain."
items.note: Reviews find small, short-lived gains in working memory and switching between tasks after time in nature (Stevenson and colleagues, 2018).
items.mind: Use nature for recovery between sessions. Do not promise better learning.
links: Use nature and daylight, and claim only what the evidence shows

items.name: Exercise and the brain
items.offers: "Exercise grows new brain cells."
items.note: One bout of exercise has a real but generally small effect on thinking (Chang and colleagues, 2012). Longer-term brain claims are promising and easy to overstate.
items.mind: Offer movement for energy. Leave brain growth out of it.
links: Use movement where it helps the learning

items.name: Amygdala hijack
items.offers: "Fear hijacks the thinking brain."
items.note: A popular phrase from Daniel Goleman's 1995 book Emotional Intelligence, not a research finding. Stress and threat do affect thinking, as the stress research shows.
items.mind: Talk about psychological safety, which has research behind it.
links: Make it safe to be wrong out loud

items.name: Rewiring the brain
items.offers: "Rewire your brain in a weekend."
items.note: All learning changes the brain in some sense. No research shows a retreat produces a special or lasting rewiring.
items.mind: Promise practice, plans and follow-up instead.
links: Promise the conditions, never the transformation

compare.heading: What to say instead
compare.intro: Brochure claims rewritten so they stay true. The right-hand column is what you can say with confidence.

rows.label: Stress
values: Stress affects memory in both directions. Brochure figures are usually wrong
"A calm, unhurried setting, with time to recover between sessions"

rows.label: Sleep
values: Sleep helps memories settle, and lost sleep harms learning
"Early finishes and quiet nights, because sleep helps learning stick"

rows.label: Reflection
values: Reflection helps learning. The brain network research is correlational
"Quiet time to think, with prompts that lead to action"

rows.label: Novelty
values: A new setting may help memory a little, mostly shown in animals
"A fresh setting away from the office"

rows.label: Bonding
values: Oxytocin and trust did not replicate. Moving together has some support
"Shared walks, meals and evenings that give the group time together"

rows.label: Change
values: No evidence for special or lasting rewiring
"Practice with feedback, a plan for the first week and a follow-up at 30 days"

mind.heading: Things to bear in mind
items: **A brain claim is a health claim.** Advertising rules expect evidence for objective claims before you publish them. There is more on [describing the retreat honestly](t:8.34).
**Most studies used students in laboratories.** Workplace and retreat evidence is much thinner.
**Brain pictures persuade more than they should.** Leave them out of proposals unless they change what you will do.
**Clients will quote brain claims to you.** Agree with what is true, correct what is not, and say what you will do instead.

business.heading: What this means for your retreats
p: **Lead with what happens.** Sleep, quiet time, practice, shared meals, walks and evenings are all easy to describe and backed by research about behaviour.
**Use one brain fact, well.** Sleep helping memory is the strongest. Use it to explain the early finishes, and stop there.
**Be the honest one.** In a market full of dopamine and cortisol, a provider who can explain what the science does and does not say will stand out to serious buyers.

sources: Shields, Sazma, McCullough and Yonelinas (2017), The effects of acute stress on episodic memory: a meta-analysis and integrative review. Psychological Bulletin, 143(6).
Immordino-Yang, Christodoulou and Singh (2012), Rest is not idleness: implications of the brain's default mode for human development and education.
Schomaker, van Bronkhorst and Meeter (2014), Exploring a novel environment improves motivation and promotes recall of words. Frontiers in Psychology.
Nave, Camerer and McCullough (2015), Does oxytocin increase trust in humans? A critical review of research. Perspectives on Psychological Science, 10(6).
Rennung and Göritz (2016), Prosocial consequences of interpersonal synchrony: a meta-analysis.
Mogan, Fischer and Bulbulia (2017), To be in synchrony or not? A meta-analysis of synchrony's effects.
Piff, Dietze, Feinberg, Stancato and Keltner (2015), Awe, the small self, and prosocial behavior. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 108(6).
Stevenson, Schilhab and Bentsen (2018), Attention restoration theory II: a systematic review.
Chang, Labban, Gapin and Etnier (2012), The effects of acute exercise on cognitive performance: a meta-analysis.
Diekelmann and Born (2010), The memory function of sleep. Nature Reviews Neuroscience.

ideas.title: Why take people away? The case for the training retreat, and what to watch
ideas.standfirst: A retreat puts a group together, away from the day job, for long enough to practise, talk and think. This is what the evidence on this site supports, what it does not, and what that means for a business built on training retreats in nature.

short.heading: The short version
items: **The strongest evidence is about what happens in the time, not the place.** Practice with feedback, reflection and debriefs, people teaching each other and a room where it is safe to be wrong. A retreat gives all four more room than a day in the office.
**The setting adds smaller benefits.** Recovery outdoors, fewer interruptions, meals and evenings together. Each has some support. None has been shown to make adults learn more.
**The biggest risk is that a retreat is one block.** Spaced learning beats massed learning in almost every comparison, so a retreat works best at the centre of a programme with a before and an after.
**Promise the conditions, never the transformation.** It is the honest offer, and it is the one a buyer can check.

sections.h: What a retreat has that a training day does not
p: **Four things set a residential apart.** Time: two or three days without a five o'clock cut-off, so practice can go round more than once and there is room to reflect. Distance: people are away from their desks, their meetings and the small interruptions of a normal day. Company: they eat, walk and spend evenings with the same group, which allows the informal contact a training room rarely does. Setting: a place chosen for the work, which can include daylight, grounds and nature.

**None of these teaches anything on its own.** Each one makes room for the methods that do. That is the case for a retreat in one line: it buys the time and the conditions for the methods with the best evidence, and adds some smaller benefits of its own.

**Practice and reflection come first.** People remember actions they perform far better than actions they only read about, and structured debriefs improved later performance by about a fifth to a quarter across 46 samples. Both need time that a single training day rarely has. There is more on [letting people do it, then reflect](t:1.27).

**Peers and safety come next.** Preparing to teach, and then teaching, helped learners in a pooling of 28 studies. In work teams, believing it is safe to take a risk goes with more learning behaviour. A group that has had dinner together and walked together usually reaches that point sooner, though nobody has measured how much sooner. There is more on [having learners teach each other](t:1.20) and on [building trust before asking for openness](t:8.3).

**Face to face and on site has some support.** A pooling of 335 samples of leadership training found that on-site and face-to-face delivery went with stronger effects. The summary does not say why or by how much, and when online and classroom courses use the same methods they teach facts equally well. The method does the work. A retreat is a good place to use the methods that need people in the same room.

**Nature helps people recover.** Reviews find small, short-lived gains in working memory and switching between tasks after time in natural settings, and some evidence for lower stress and less brooding. That makes time outdoors a good use of the space between demanding sessions. It is not a teaching method. There is more on [using nature and daylight](t:1.16) and on [using the outdoors on a retreat](t:8.27).

**Fewer interruptions take pressure off.** In one experiment, people who were interrupted worked faster but reported more stress, frustration and time pressure. The popular claim that a phone on the table drains brainpower did not survive two direct replications, so ask for phones away because the group deserves full attention, not because of brain science.

**Meals, evenings and fires bring people together.** Firefighter platoons that ate together more often were rated higher for team performance. Among the Ju/'hoan of the Kalahari, talk by the fire at night was mostly stories, while daytime talk was mostly about practical matters and complaints. Both findings are interesting and neither tested training. They are the strongest support we found for what many retreat leaders already believe: the shared meal and the evening fire are where a group gets to know itself.

sections.h: The catch: one block of learning
p: **Massed learning loses to spaced learning.** Across 271 comparisons of massed and spaced study, all but 12 favoured spacing. A retreat is massed by design. A residential is not a memory experiment, but the direction is clear enough that two days with nothing after them is a poor bet.

**The answer is to design the before and the after.** Pre-work and a manager briefing before. Two or three days away. Spaced follow-ups, a peer group and a check on use at work after. The leadership training pooling found spaced sessions also went with stronger effects. There is more on [what a retreat can and cannot do](t:8.8) and on [planning the return to work](t:8.17).

dashboard.heading: The evidence at a glance
dashboard.intro: Eighteen things that make a retreat different, each with the most useful figure we found, how strong the research behind it is, and what to bear in mind. The strength rating is about the evidence for that element, not about whether it is worth doing. Some of the best parts of a retreat rest on craft.

items.name: Together, face to face
items.offers: People in one room can watch, practise and correct each other in real time.
items.note: samples of leadership training pooled by Lacerenza and colleagues (2017). On-site and face-to-face delivery went with stronger effects. The summary does not say why or by how much.
items.mind: When the methods match, online and classroom courses teach facts equally well. The method does the work.
links: Know whether online training works as well as the classroom
Know what the evidence says a retreat can and cannot do

items.name: Away from distraction
items.offers: Fewer messages, meetings and small demands pulling at attention.
items.note: People interrupted during a task worked faster but reported more stress, frustration and time pressure (Mark, Gudith and Klocke, 2008, a laboratory experiment).
items.mind: The claim that a phone on the table drains brainpower failed two direct replications. Ask for phones away for the group's sake.
links: Set the rules for phones and contact with work
Design for people who arrive distracted

items.name: Time and absorption
items.offers: Long blocks where the challenge can be matched to each person's skill.
items.note: studies pooled by Fong and colleagues (2015): a moderate link between challenge matched to skill and reported flow, weaker in work and education settings.
items.mind: Intensity is not learning. An activity that photographs well is not necessarily one that teaches.
links: Design for absorption, not intensity

items.name: Hands-on practice
items.offers: Doing the real task, more than once, with feedback.
items.note: A large review found people remember actions they perform better than actions they only read about (Roberts, MacLeod and Fernandes, 2022).
items.mind: Make the movement the content. A stretch does nothing for the skill. Doing the task does.
links: Use movement where it helps the learning
Make practice harder in the ways that help

items.name: Group work and peer teaching
items.offers: People explain, question and give feedback to each other.
items.note: studies pooled on learning by teaching (Kobayashi, 2019) and on peer assessment (Double and colleagues, 2020). Both found gains.
items.mind: Peers can pass on errors with confidence. Review the key points with the whole group afterwards.
links: Have learners teach each other

items.name: Reflection and debrief
items.offers: Protected time to say what happened and what it means for work.
items.note: better later performance after structured debriefs, across 46 samples (Tannenbaum and Cerasoli, 2013). Most studies were not full experiments.
items.mind: The activity always wants to overrun. Protect the debrief time in the plan.
links: Let people do it, then make them reflect

items.name: Safety and trust
items.offers: A group where people can ask, admit mistakes and try half-formed ideas.
items.note: teams in a manufacturing company: believing it was safe to take a risk went with more learning behaviour (Edmondson, 1999).
items.mind: Everyone is working out what gets back to their manager. State the reporting rule before any exercise.
links: Make it safe to be wrong out loud
Build trust before you ask for openness

items.name: Community and connection
items.offers: Contacts across teams that last beyond the event.
items.note: LinkedIn users in experiments that found moderately weak ties did the most for job moves (Rajkumar and colleagues, 2022).
items.mind: The research is about jobs and ideas, not courses. Give each connection a job and a reason to meet again.
links: Know that people learn through their network
Design the course so people leave connected

items.name: Nature and the outdoors
items.offers: Recovery between demanding sessions and a setting for reflection and conversation.
items.note: newer studies reviewed in 2018: low to moderate, short-term gains in working memory and switching between tasks after time in nature (Stevenson and colleagues).
items.mind: No study shows that nature makes adults learn a skill better. Use it for recovery and conversation, with a wet-weather plan.
links: Use nature and daylight, and claim only what the evidence shows
Use the outdoors on a retreat, on purpose

items.name: Movement and exercise
items.offers: A lift in energy, and a way to learn physical tasks by doing them.
items.note: A pooled analysis found that one bout of exercise has a real but generally small effect on thinking (Chang and colleagues, 2012).
items.mind: Optional, with a seated version, and never sold as brain science.
links: Offer movement sessions people can choose
Use movement where it helps the learning

items.name: Sleep
items.offers: Nights between the sessions, when new memories settle.
items.note: Pooled studies: a lost night before learning weakens taking in new material, and a lost night after weakens keeping it (Newbury and colleagues, 2021).
items.mind: The programme must never demand a late night. Acas counts training needed for the job as working time.
links: Protect sleep on multi-day programmes
Set the rules for evenings, alcohol and free time

items.name: Good food, eaten together
items.offers: Shared meals that keep people talking.
items.note: fire service supervisors rated platoons that ate together more often higher for team performance (Kniffin and colleagues, 2015). A correlation, not a trial.
items.mind: A co-author later had many other papers retracted. We found no retraction of this one, but treat it with care. We found no good evidence for "brain food" claims for adults. Keep lunch light and on time.
links: Run evenings and fireside conversations
The slot after lunch

items.name: Play
items.offers: Low-stakes ways to try things, mix people and enjoy the time.
items.note: A 2018 review called play in adult learning under-explored, with no settled line of research (Whitton).
items.mind: Optional, or it becomes a task. Name its purpose: mixing people, a point to debrief, or simply fun.
links: Use play on purpose, not as a break
Bring play into a retreat without losing the point

items.name: Guest speakers
items.offers: A practitioner's story, a demonstration, a view from outside.
items.note: We found no research on guest speakers in workplace training. Learning by watching skilled people is well established, which is the case for a speaker who shows rather than tells.
items.mind: Brief them on the outcome. Keep the talk to 20 minutes and spend the rest on the group's questions.
links: Give a ten-minute input
Demonstrate a skill

items.name: Fireside conversation
items.offers: An unhurried evening circle where stories come out.
items.note: of night-time talk around the fire among the Ju/'hoan of the Kalahari was stories, against 6% of daytime talk (Wiessner, 2014). One society, studied by anthropology.
items.mind: Optional, with no confession on demand. Check the venue's fire rules and put the fire in the risk assessment.
links: Run evenings and fireside conversations
Build trust before you ask for openness

items.name: Thresholds and ritual
items.offers: A marked start and end that tell people the rules have changed.
items.note: Liminality is an anthropologist's idea (Turner, 1969), borrowed by retreat designers. It has not been tested as a cause of change.
items.mind: Keep it plain: one sentence each, and let people pass. Ceremony can feel forced at work.
links: Take people out of their routine, and plan the return

items.name: Spacing: the catch
items.offers: What a single block cannot give: returns to the material over weeks.
items.note: average recall for spaced against massed study, across 271 comparisons. All but 12 favoured spacing (Cepeda and colleagues, 2006).
items.mind: A retreat is massed learning. Put it at the centre of a programme with spaced follow-ups.
links: Know what the evidence says a retreat can and cannot do
Space and mix the practice, then stop drilling

items.name: The return to work
items.offers: Plans, managers and follow-up that get the learning used.
items.note: studies pooled on transfer: ability, motivation and a supportive workplace were linked to people using training at work (Blume and colleagues, 2010).
items.mind: The budget usually ends at checkout. Sell the follow-up with the retreat.
links: Plan the return to work
Treat transfer as a design problem

compare.heading: How a retreat compares
compare.intro: The same programme in three formats. These are general patterns, not research findings, except where the last row says so.

rows.label: Distance from daily work
values: Low. Work is one tab away

rows.label: Spacing
values: Needs a designed before and after

rows.label: What the research says
values: Equal to the classroom when methods match
The comparison point in most studies
On-site went with stronger effects in leadership training. The cause is unknown

mind.heading: Things to bear in mind
items: **One block is the weakest design.** Sell and plan the before and the after with the retreat, not as an extra.
**Promise the conditions, never the transformation.** List what will happen and what people will leave with. There is more on [promising the conditions](t:8.1).

**Not everyone can stay away.** Caring responsibilities, health, faith and preference all count. Design a day-attendance version from the start, as in [including people who cannot stay overnight](t:8.16).
**Evenings carry the most risk.** Alcohol, late nights and managers in the bar. The conduct rules are the client's to set, and [the evening rules](t:8.14) set out how.

**Cost, travel and carbon add up.** A residential costs the most per head, and every hour of travel is an hour of someone's weekend or working day. Aim for under two hours' travel and shared transport. There is more on [costing it](t:8.13) and on [cutting the travel and carbon](t:8.33).
**The setting is not the method.** Plan the sessions before you fall for the view.

**Check every claim in the brochure.** "Nature boosts creativity by 50 per cent", "digital detox restores the brain" and "only 10 per cent of training transfers" all fail when traced to their source. There is more on [describing the retreat honestly](t:8.34) and in [the neuroscience myth check](insight:neuroscience-of-the-retreat).

**The seasons change the design.** In a British winter there are about eight hours of daylight, so outdoor blocks go in the middle of the day and every one needs a wet-weather version. There is more on [planning for the season](t:8.28).
**Measure what people do at work.** Satisfaction forms will be glowing after a good retreat and say little about change. There is more on [measuring what people do differently](t:6.4).

business.heading: What this means for a retreat business
p: **Lead with the methods and the time.** Present the setting as what makes them possible. A buyer can always find a cheaper day course. The honest answer to "why pay more?" is unbroken time for practice and reflection, a group that gets to know each other, and recovery built into the day.

**Sell a programme, not an event.** Pre-work and a manager briefing before, two or three days away, then spaced follow-ups and a peer group after. That answers the spacing problem, and it gives you a reason to stay in touch with the client.

**Design nature, food, sleep and evenings.** They are where a retreat in nature differs most from a hotel conference room, and where the claims need the most care. Put them in the timetable with a purpose, not just in the brochure.
**Promise conditions you can show you delivered.** Then measure what people do at work three months later. That is what earns the second booking.
